header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
body: SHAHRUKH ARJUMAND, J.- Through Jail Appeal No.141/2023, the appellant, Adil Ahmed alias Adeel, calls into question his conviction under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”), and sentence of imprisonment for life, together with compensation of Rs.500,000 under Section 544-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.P.C.”) vide judgment dated 21.03.2023 (“Impugned Judgment”) passed by the learned Additional sessions Judge, Islamabad (East), arising out of FIR No.35, dated 22-02-2017, registered under Appellant by Respondent/ Complainant by State by Date of hearing : M/s Talat Mehmood Zaidi and Faisal Nawaz Advocates.
: M/s Jan Muhammad Khan and Raza Ali Shah Advocates.
Complainant in person.
: Mr. Nisar Shah, State Counsel.
Mr. Muhammad Sharif ASI/IO, with record.

Page-2 Sections 302, 324, 148, 149, 337-F(i) and 337-F(ii) PPC at Police Station Khanna, Islamabad. Whereas, Criminal Appeal No.145/2023 has been filed by the complainant in terms of section 417(2A) Cr.P.C. assailing acquittal of the accused Sher Bahadur, Khan Bahadur and Dilawar Khan vide the Impugned Judgment and Criminal Revision No. 59/22023 has also been filed by the complainant praying enhancement of sentence awarded to appellant Adil Ahmed alias Adeel to death and reasonable amount of compensation.

2. The prosecution’s version, as set out in the FIR, is that the complainant, Faja Akbar, had rented premises where a school and an evening academy for girls were established. Certain persons allegedly used to harass the girls attending the academy, and the complainant’s son, Usman, had repeatedly warned them to refrain from such conduct. On 22-02-2017, Adil and Nasibullah allegedly stood at the main chowk, where an exchange of hot words took place with Usman. They thereafter departed while threatening to teach him a lesson. Usman returned home and asked the complainant/his father to accompany him to inform their families. The complainant, along with Usman, Shah Akbar and Zia-ul-Haq, were proceeding towards the academy. At approximately 05:30 p.m., near its gate, they allegedly encountered the appellant and other accused persons armed with churis, lathis and dandas. During the ensuing assault, Usman sustained successive churi blows, including blows on his chest and below his armpit by hands of Adil and Naseebullah accused. Upon hearing hue and cry, Mumtaz Khan, Iqbal Khan and Badruddin approached the place of occurrence and were also injured while attempting to intervene. The accused persons allegedly fled, whereafter the complainant party shifted the deceased and injured persons to PIMS Hospital. The complainant’s verbal account was recorded at the hospital and transmitted to the police station for registration of the FIR.

3. The charge against the appellant and the other accused persons was framed on 17-05-2017, whereas the accused, Rabnawaz, was charged on 21-07-2017. The prosecution examined the following fourteen witnesses in support of its case.
1. PW-1: Faja Akbar, complainant.
2. PW-2: Mumtaz Khan, injured eyewitness.
Page-3 3. PW-3: Iqbal Khan, injured eyewitness.
4. PW-4: Badruddin, injured eyewitness.
5. PW-5: Amir Shehzad, draftsman.
6. PW-6: Shah Akbar, eyewitness and attesting witness to recovery proceedings.
7. PW-7: Zaheer Ahmed, Constable, witness concerning proclamation proceedings and transmission of case property.
8. PW-8: Muhammad Abid, Constable No.249/C, witness concerning transmission of case property.
9. PW-9: Falak Naz, SI, investigating officer and witness to the recovery of Exh.P-14.
10.PW-10: Dr. Farrukh Kamal, MLO PIMS 11.PW-11: Riyaz Hussain, witness concerning custody of case property in the malkhana.
12.PW-12: Naveed Tahir, SI, witness concerning weapon recoveries.
13.PW-13: Ahmed Kamal, Inspector, investigating officer.
14.PW-14: Muhammad Abbas, SI.

The gist of material prosecution witnesses is as follows.-  The complainant, Fajja Akbar (PW-1), reiterated the FIR version concerning harassment of the academy’s female students, the earlier quarrel and the subsequent assault upon his son, Usman. He also witnessed recovery proceedings and identified the deceased’s dead body. During cross-examination, he admitted that he was not present during the earlier exchange of hot words; that the accused persons were already at the spot when he arrived; that his son received injuries; and that the FIR was registered approximately two and a half hours after the occurrence. He stated that he accompanied the deceased and injured persons to the hospital in the same vehicle. He subsequently nominated Usman, Rabnawaz and Noman, initially described as unknown, and admitted that no identification parade was held in his presence.

 Mumtaz Khan (PW-2), an injured witness, attributed churi blows upon himself to Usman, Mansha and Rabnawaz. He subsequently nominated Nauman, Usman and Rabnawaz through a supplementary statement recorded on 06.03.2017. During cross-examination, he denied knowing Qari Wasim and expressed ignorance about his Page-4 having sustained injuries. He admitted that the accused persons were already present when the witnesses reached the spot.

 Iqbal Khan (PW-3), another injured witness, stated that he, Mumtaz and Badar Din emerged from their houses upon hearing hue and cry and saw Nasibullah and Mansha inflicting churi blows upon the deceased. He attributed his own hand and chest injuries to Rabnawaz (since PO). He nominated Noman, Usman and Rabnawaz through a supplementary statement dated 06-03-2017. During crossexamination, he stated that the occurrence took place between Asr and Maghrib prayers, approximately 6-7 yards from the opening of their street onto the main road, and that he traced the previously unknown accused persons’ names within six to eight days of the occurrence.  Badar Deen (PW-4), also an injured witness, attributed a churi blow upon himself to Usman accused. Through his supplementary statement dated 06-03-2017, he nominated Noman, Usman and Rabnawaz. During cross-examination, he admitted that the place of occurrence became visible only after he reached the main road. He gave varying estimates of the distance between his house and that road and stated that he traced the previously unknown accused persons’ names within three to four days.

 Shah Akbar (PW-6), the complainant’s son-in-law, stated that he accompanied the complainant and deceased when the occurrence took place at approximately 05:30 p.m. He witnessed collection of blood through cotton from the deceased’s dead body in the emergency ward of PIMS Hospital and attested recovery proceedings. During crossexamination, he admitted that he was not present during the earlier quarrel. He stated that, during the stabbing, he stood approximately three yards away, with the complainant beside him and Zia-ul-Haq behind him. He knew Qari Waseem but had not seen him at the spot. According to him, the complainant and injured persons travelled in one vehicle, while he accompanied other persons in another.

 Amir Shehzad (PW-5), Draftsman, prepared the scaled site plan after visiting the spot on 03-03-2017 on the instructions of the complainant Page-5 and investigating officer. He admitted that relevant houses, their distances from the place of occurrence and their inter se distances were omitted from the plan.

 Falak Naz (PW-9), SI, witnessed the alleged recovery of the churi (Exh.P-14) at the instance of Adil Ahmed on 08-03-2017. He explained the date 08-02-2017 on the recovery memo as a clerical mistake and was cross-examined by the prosecution as hostile. He admitted that documentary evidence concerning Ahmed Kamal’s medical condition was unavailable, although he had mentioned it in a case diary. He described preparation of the weapon parcel at the recovery spot and denied that Ahmed Kamal prepared it on 08-03- 2017. The postmortem report names him as a person who brought the dead body, but he did not explain that entry in his testimony.  Riyaz Hussain (PW-11), the Moharrar malkhana, stated that he received the churi parcel from Falak Naz on 08-03-2017 and the knife parcel from Ahmed Kamal on 28-04-2017 for safe custody. During cross-examination, he was confronted with his statement dated 09-03- 2017, which did not mention a blood-stained chhuri. He admitted that the parcels were entrusted to different carriers.

 Naveed Tahir (PW-12), SI, testified concerning the weapon recoveries at the instance of Adil and Rabnawaz. He stated that Adil led to recovery of the chhuri on 08-03-2017 and that the police travelled to the recovery location in an official single-cabin Tata vehicle bearing registration No.GAC-6-18.

 Ahmed Kamal (PW-13), Inspector, stated that the deceased’s dead body was already at PIMS Hospital when he arrived. He collected blood from the stretcher, prepared the inquest report and application for conducting postmortem, conducted investigation and forwarded the weapon parcels to PFSA on 05-05-2017. During crossexamination, he admitted that he found no blood marks or recoverable evidence during his spot inspection; examined no student, school representative or owner; obtained neither the attendance register nor the rent agreement; and did not send the knife for DNA grouping with Page-6 the deceased. He also admitted that the complaint did not specify the time of the earlier quarrel.

 Zaheer Ahmed Constable (PW-7), and Muhammad Abid Constable (PW-8), testified relating transmission of case property to PFSA. Zaheer Ahmed also described bringing a parcel back and depositing it with the Moharrar Malkhana. Although identified as the carrier of the complaint from the hospital to the police station, but did not depose such fact in his statement as witness and also the fact of his accompany the investigating officer to the hospital.

 Dr. Farrukh Kamal (PW10) conducted the autopsy and examined the injured witnesses. The postmortem was conducted at 10:30 p.m., and the estimated interval between death and postmortem was three to five hours (over writing noted). The postmortem report records that the body was brought by Ahmed Kamal Inspector and Falak Naz SI and identified by Shah Akbar and Shabzal Khan. The death certificate (Exh.PL) records admission at 06:59 p.m. on 22-02-2017, with the remarks “brought dead”.

4. The appellant’s statement under Section 342 Cr.P.C. was recorded on 17-12- 2022, wherein he disputed the incriminating evidence, including the alleged recovery of the chhuri. Upon conclusion of the trial, Sher Bahadur, Khan Bahadur and Dilawar Khan were acquitted, while the appellant was convicted and sentenced as stated above.

5. Learned counsel for the appellant contended that the prosecution failed to establish his guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that the learned trial court did not properly appreciate the material discrepancies in its evidence. He submitted that the complainant and other eyewitnesses claimed to have transported the deceased to the hospital within twenty to twenty-five minutes of the occurrence at 05:30 p.m., whereas the death certificate recorded admission at 06:59 p.m. with the remarks “brought dead”. He further argued that the postmortem report named Ahmed Kamal, Inspector, and Falak Naz, SI, as the persons who brought the dead body, although both officers stated that it had already reached the hospital when Page-7 they arrived. According to him, these discrepancies cast doubt upon the witnesses’ account of the immediate aftermath of the occurrence. He also questioned the unexplained delay in registration of the FIR, particularly when Zaheer Ahmed, Constable, did not confirm carrying the complaint from the hospital to the police station. He maintained that the alleged harassment of students and earlier quarrel were not independently established, while the discrepancies concerning the recovery, description, custody and transmission of the alleged weapon deprived it of reliable corroborative value. He accordingly sought acquittal by extending the benefit of doubt.

6. Conversely, learned counsel for the complainant and the learned State counsel supported the impugned judgment, submitting that the complainant’s account was supported by injured eyewitnesses whose presence at the occurrence was established by their injuries. They maintained that the medical evidence was consistent with the alleged assault and that the recovery of the weapon furnished further support to the prosecution’s case. They argued that the discrepancies concerning hospital particulars, approximate timings and recovery documentation did not undermine the substantive account of the assault, and that the reporting interval had to be considered in light of the immediate necessity of shifting the deceased and injured persons to the hospital. They further submitted that the acquittal of co-accused assigned different roles did not warrant the appellant’s acquittal and sought dismissal of the appeal.

7. The principal question is whether the prosecution established the appellant’s participation in the fatal assault through reliable evidence sufficient to exclude reasonable doubt. This question requires examination of five connected aspects: the eyewitnesses’ opportunity of observation; their account of the deceased’s transportation and hospital arrival; the recording and transmission of the initial accusation; the support available from the medical evidence; and the connection established through the alleged recovery and forensic examination.

8. The prosecution case is supported by the ocular account furnished by Faja Akbar (PW-1), Mumtaz Khan (PW-2), Iqbal Khan (PW-3) and Badruddin (PW-4). Except for the complainant, the remaining three witnesses allegedly sustained Page-8 injuries in the alleged scuffle while attempting to free the deceased from the clutches of the accused persons. Mumtaz Khan (PW-2) attributed his injuries to Usman, Mansha and Rabnawaz, all proclaimed offenders. Iqbal Khan (PW-3) attributed his injury to Rabnawaz, whereas Badar Din (PW-4) attributed his injury to Usman. The complainant attributed the fatal churi blow on the deceased’s chest to Adil and below the deceased’s armpit to Naseebullah.

9. The entire prosecution story revolves around a dispute arising from an academy allegedly established in the plaza owned by the complainant. However, no evidence was brought on record to establish that the premises had been rented to the academy, that it had started functioning within a week of the execution of the alleged rent agreement, or that boys thereafter used to stand in front of it to tease the female students. Admittedly, neither the complainant nor the injured witnesses had witnessed the initial altercation between the deceased and the accused persons, which led to the occurrence.

10. The complainant claimed his presence at the place of occurrence and thereafter at the hospital, which was also asserted by the injured witnesses. However, the postmortem report records that the deceased’s dead body was brought to the hospital by Ahmed Kamal, Inspector, and Falak Naz, Sub-Inspector, and identified by Shah Akbar and Shabzal Khan. The complainant’s name does not appear in the relevant column despite his claimed presence. Furthermore, Falak Naz SI did not utter a single word in his testimony to affirm that he had brought the dead body to the hospital, as recorded in the postmortem report.

11. According to the eyewitnesses, the occurrence took place at 05:30 p.m., and they took the dead body to the hospital within 20–25 minutes. However, the death certificate records the deceased’s admission at 06:59 p.m. on 22-02-2017, with the remarks “brought dead”. This timing is inconsistent with the time of arrival stated by the eyewitnesses. Admittedly, the FIR was registered approximately two and a half hours after the occurrence, despite the complainant’s claimed presence at the place of occurrence and thereafter at the hospital throughout with the injured and the deceased. The prosecution has not furnished any explanation for the delay in Page-9 registration of the FIR. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the recent judgment Asia Bibi v. The State, etc. (PLD 2019 SC 64) addressed the delay in registration of the FIR in the following manner:

“In this regard reference has been made by the learned counsel for the complainant on the judgments of this Court reported as Zar Bahadar Vs. the State (1978 SCMR 136) and Sheraz Asghar Vs. the State (1995 SCMR 1365) to contend that the delay in registration of a FIR is not per se fatal in all the cases as it never washes away nor torpedoes trustworthy and reliable ocular and circumstantial evidence. There is no cavil to the proposition, however, it is to be noted that in absence of any plausible explanation, this Court has always considered the delay in lodging of FIR to be fatal and castes a suspicion on the prosecution story, extending the benefit of doubt to the accused. It has been held by this Court that a FIR is always treated as a cornerstone of the prosecution case to establish guilt against those involved in a crime; thus, it has a significant role to play. If there is any delay in lodging of a FIR and commencement of investigation, it gives rise to a doubt, which, of course, cannot be extended to anyone else except to the accused. Furthermore, FIR lodged after conducting an inquiry loses its evidentiary value. [see: Iftikhar Hussain and others Vs. The State (2004 SCMR 1185)] Reliance in this behalf may also be made to the case titled as Zeeshan @ Shani Vs. The State (2012 SCMR 428) wherein it was held that delay of more than one hour in lodging the FIR give rise to the inference that occurrence did not take place in the manner projected by prosecution and time was consumed in making effort to give a coherent attire to prosecution case, which hardly proved successful. Such a delay is even more fatal when the police station, besides being connected with the scene of occurrence through a metaled road, was at a distance of 11 kilometers from the latter. In the case titled as Noor Muhammad Vs. The State (2010 SCMR 97) it was held that when the prosecution could not furnish any plausible explanation for the delay of twelve hours in lodging the FIR, which time appeared to have been spent in consultation and preparation of the case, the same was fatal to the prosecution case. In the case titled as Muhammad Fiaz Khan Vs. Ajmer Khan (2010 SCMR 105) it was held that when complaint is filed after a considerable delay, which was not explained by complainant then in such situation it raises suspicion as to its truthfulness. Thus, we are of the view that in the facts and Page-10 circumstances of the case, the explanation given by the prosecution is not plausible.”

12. According to the FIR and the testimony of Ahmed Kamal, Inspector, he visited the hospital with his team, comprising Zaheer Ahmed and other officials. The complaint was transmitted from the hospital to the police station for registration of the FIR through Constable Zaheer Ahmed, who entered the witness box but did not depose to this fact. Furthermore, none of the other members of Ahmed Kamal’s team entered the witness box to support the prosecution version. Thus the statement of the investigating officer relating to dispatch of the complaint to the police station from the hospital remained uncorroborated, whereas, the prosecution itself did not examine the other team members, which definitely attract the negative inference embedded in Article 129(g) of the Qanoon-e-Shahat Order, 1984. Reliance is placed on the case of Ghulam Rasool v. The State (2025 SCMR 74).

13. Ahmed Kamal, Inspector, further stated that he did not collect any evidence, including blood-stained earth, from the alleged place of occurrence to establish that the occurrence had actually taken place there. The Investigating Officer (PW-13) admitted during cross examination that “I never observed any mark of blood on the said place of occurrence. During my spot inspection at the place of occurrence, I did not find andy such piece of evidence which is to be secured under a seizure memo.” Rather, as per Exh.PA, recovery memo of blood stained cotton, the sample was obtained from the strecher in the emergency ward of PIMS. In the case titled Rafaqat Ali alias Foji and another v. The State and others (2024 SCMR 1579), the blood sample was obtained from underneath the cot of the deceased in a medical facility whereupon the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that omission to secure blood stained earth from the crime scene created serious doubts as to the place of occurrence as narrated by the prosecution witnesses.

14. The entire dispute between the accused and the complainant party had been due to the female students of Falcon Academy allegedly established in the plaza rented by the complainant. Even half of the portion of the FIR, complaint, Page-11 statement of complainant and other witnesses centers around the Falcon Academy. Nothing was adduced into evidence regarding the ownership, tenancy and the establishment of the said academy. The prosecution also failed to produce any of the staff members of the said academy in support of the complainant’s version. Furthermore, no witness of the scuffle that allegedly took place before the occurrence between the deceased and accused persons was examined in support of the prosecution’s version. In addition, neither the prosecution obtained any kind of CCTV footage nor produced before the trial court. This would have been of utmost significance in the present case, as the failure of the prosecution to collect blood stained soil from the crime scene and any other kind of corroborating evidence, has already rendered the place of occurrence doubtful.

15. During cross-examination, the complainant admitted that Qari Waseem had sustained injuries during the occurrence but had not been taken to the hospital. Despite this admission, the complainant denied that Qari Waseem was known to him. Significantly, the latter was neither nominated as an accused, whether by name or otherwise, nor was his identity, status or role in the occurrence explained by the complainant. He was not identified as an accused, a passerby, or a member of the complainant’s own party. This deliberate omission assumes significance, as the complainant, while acknowledging the presence and injuries of Qari Waseem, withheld the very particulars necessary to establish his identity and connection with the occurrence. The complainant’s failure to disclose these material facts gives rise to a legitimate inference that he has suppressed the identity and role of a material person whose presence could have shed light on the true genesis and manner of the occurrence. The investigating Officer also remained fail to investigate this aspect of the case. In these circumstances, Qari Waseem was a material witness, and his non-production by the prosecution, without any plausible explanation, attracts the adverse presumption under Article 129(g) of the Qanun-e- Shahadat Order, 1984. It may reasonably be presumed that, had he been produced, his testimony would not have supported the prosecution version. This omission, read with the complainant’s unexplained concealment of his identity, casts a further shadow of doubt upon the prosecution case.

Page-12 16. Malik Amir Shahzad (PW-05) admitted that he did not show the complainant’s house in the scaled site plan (Exh.PF) or its distance from the place of occurrence, whereas he showed the houses of PWs Mumtaz Khan, Iqbal Khan and Badar Din and their respective distances. A perusal of Exh.PF shows that it depicts the picture of entire area adjacent to Falcon Academy. According to the complainant’s own version recorded in the FIR, he had purchased the plaza and started residing nearby in a rented house. Had this statement been true, the scaled site plan would have shown the house rented by him. This omission is particularly significant because Exh.PF is sufficiently detailed to depict the houses of the eyewitnesses, making it implausible that the draftsman would have omitted the complainant’s house situated nearby.

17. The conduct of the complainant, Faja Akbar, who is the father of the deceased, and the other eyewitnesses, Shah Akbar and Zia ul Haq, also is questionable. Shah Akbar claimed that the he alongwith the two witnesses were standing at a distance of merely three yards from the deceased when the accused stabbed the deceased, yet nothing came on record to show that they or the complainant attempted to intervene or rescue the deceased. The complainant’s failure to make even an unsuccessful attempt to save his own son remains unexplained. In Muhammad Asif v. The State (2017 SCMR 486), the Hon’ble Supreme Court questioned the presence of parents and close companions who claimed to have witnessed a dagger attack from nearby but did not intervene to rescue the deceased.

18. Although the complainant named the accused persons Sher Bahadur, Khan Bahadur and Dilawar Khan in the FIR as having caused injuries to PWs, but while recording his statement before the trial court as PW-1, did not assign them any injury nor any role in the commission of offence. Likewise, the other eye witnesses also did not assign any role to these accused persons. In the facts and circumstances, the learned trial court rightly acquitted them from the charge, which conclusion does not warrant interference.

19. Viewed cumulatively, the unexplained delay in registration of the FIR, the inconsistencies concerning the deceased’s transportation and arrival at the hospital, Page-13 the doubtful presence and conduct of the eyewitnesses, and the absence of reliable physical evidence establishing the alleged place of occurrence materially undermine the prosecution case. The alleged motive remained unproved. The presence of these material inconsistencies in the case renders it unsafe to sustain the appellant’s conviction. It is settled principle of law that when the prosecution’s case is not free from doubt, the benefit of doubt must accrue in favour of the accused as a matter of right. Reliance is placed on the cases of Muhammad Akram v. The State (2009 SCMR 230), Tariq Pervez v. The State (1995 SCMR 1345) and Muhammad Akram v. The State (2009 SCMR 230).

20. For what has been discussed above, the instant criminal appeal against conviction is ALLOWED; the impugned judgment is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted of the charge by extending him the benefit of doubt. He shall be released forthwith, if not required to be detained in any other case. For the same reasons, the Criminal Appeal No. 145/2023 against acquittal and Criminal Revision No. 59/2023 for enhancement of sentence of appellant are DISMISSED. (INAAM AMEEN MINHAS) (SHAHRUKH ARJUMAND)
